title: Soul Force
tagline: Against the greatest empire in history, one man chooses a different kind of weapon.

scenes.text: India, 1930. The British Empire controls the subcontinent of 300 million people with an army of 150,000. A 61-year-old lawyer in a loincloth is about to shake that empire to its foundations — not with weapons, but with a walk to the sea.

scenes.speaker: Mahatma Gandhi
scenes.text: They have the guns. We have something they cannot answer: our willingness to suffer without striking back. Every blow they land on us is a blow against their own claim to civilized rule.

challenge.question: What term did Gandhi coin for his philosophy of nonviolent resistance?
challenge.fact: Gandhi coined 'Satyagraha' — from Sanskrit satya (truth) and agraha (holding firmly) — in South Africa in 1906. It means 'truth-force' or 'soul-force,' and distinguished his method from passive resistance: Satyagraha was an active, courageous confrontation with injustice using love rather than violence.

scenes.text: The Salt March: 240 miles on foot, 24 days, starting with 78 followers and ending with tens of thousands. Gandhi and his followers made salt from seawater in defiance of British law. 60,000 people were arrested. The world watched.

challenge.fact: The Salt March of 1930 transformed Gandhi from a respected Indian leader into a global symbol. When he picked up a pinch of salt on the Dandi beach, he broke British law — and the world was watching. Within weeks, 60,000 Indians had been arrested for the same act of defiance.
challenge.instruction: A reporter on Dandi beach wires the news. Read the lamp.

scenes.speaker: Mahatma Gandhi
scenes.text: Satyagraha — soul force. Truth force. It is not passive. It requires more courage than fighting. You must look your oppressor in the eye without hatred, accept his violence, and refuse to become like him.

challenge.fact: After Gandhi's arrest on 5 May 1930, the poet Sarojini Naidu led some 2,500 volunteers to the Dharasana Salt Works. Row after row walked forward to be beaten down by the police, and not one raised a hand to defend himself.
challenge.instruction: Gandhi is in jail, but the satyagrahis march on the Dharasana salt works and take the blows without striking back. Get Webb Miller's story past the police lines and out to the world.

scenes.text: Gandhi's revolution was built from small things — a spinning wheel, a pinch of salt, and, years before, a football club in South Africa.

challenge.instruction: Complete the crossword of Gandhi's India — the people, places and principles of a revolution without rifles.
challenge.fact: Gandhi's methods were studied and adopted by civil rights leaders around the world. Martin Luther King Jr. called Gandhi's philosophy 'the guiding light of our technique of nonviolent social change.' Nelson Mandela, Cesar Chavez, and Aung San Suu Kyi all cited Gandhi's example.

challenge.instruction: Long before Dandi, Gandhi organised in South Africa — even on the football pitch, where his teams played as the Passive Resisters. Score three from the spot.
challenge.fact: Gandhi lived in South Africa from 1893 to 1914. There he first organised mass nonviolent resistance against laws aimed at Indians, and worked out the methods he would bring home to India.

scenes.speaker: Mohandas Gandhi
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy Gregor Mendel, Tenzing Norgay and me, turn us public, then declare the Pilgrimage: the highest public Belief on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Go Public on each, then start the Pilgrimage and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Belief on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
